s: D. Reconstruction Amendments and congressional enforcement.
Section 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment (with § 2 of the Thirteenth and Fifteenth) gives Congress power to "enforce" the amendment "by appropriate legislation."
Remedy, not redefinition.
City of Boerne v. Flores (1997) held that Congress may enact prophylactic legislation reaching some constitutional conduct to deter or remedy violations.
It may not change the substantive meaning of the amendment.
The Religious Freedom Restoration Act, which tried to restore strict scrutiny after Employment Division v. Smith, exceeded § 5 as applied to the states (it still binds the federal government).
Congruence and proportionality.
Courts compare the scope of the remedy to a record of constitutional violations.
Laws protecting classes that receive only rational-basis review generally fail: age discrimination in Kimel (2000) and Title I of the ADA (disability, employment) in Garrett (2001).

Laws addressing heightened-scrutiny classifications or fundamental rights fare better: the FMLA family-leave provision (sex discrimination) in Hibbs (2003), and Title II of the ADA as applied to access to courts in Tennessee v. Lane (2004).
Private conduct.
Section 5 reaches state action, not private conduct (Civil Rights Cases, 1883; United States v. Morrison, 2000).
The Thirteenth Amendment, by contrast, reaches private "badges and incidents of slavery" (Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co., 1968).
Fifteenth Amendment.
South Carolina v. Katzenbach (1966) upheld the Voting Rights Act's preclearance regime under a "rational means" standard.
Shelby County v. Holder (2013) held the coverage formula unconstitutional because it rested on decades-old data, invoking the "equal sovereignty" of the states.
Section 3.
In Trump v. Anderson (2024), the Court held that states may not enforce Section 3's insurrection disqualification against federal officeholders and candidates; enforcement rests with Congress.
Section 5 enforcement legislation (Boerne).
Identify the constitutional right Congress is enforcing, as the Court has defined it.
Examine the legislative record of constitutional violations by states.
Ask whether the remedy is congruent and proportional to that pattern of violations.
For damages claims against states, confirm clear abrogation of sovereign immunity.
